title: Pharmacies fed mostly by one prescriber
question: Which San Francisco pharmacies drew three quarters or more of their Medicaid drug money through a single prescribing number?
finding: Of 20 San Francisco pharmacies with $250,000 or more of Medicaid drug money in 2018-2024, 5 drew three quarters or more of it through one prescribing number; the middle pharmacy drew 50% through its largest prescriber. The largest is SCRIPTSITE PHARMACY PARTNERS LLC: 77% of $2.3 million through one number (individual clinician).
how: The national file (21,515,000 rows, one per billing number, prescribing number, drug code and month, 2018 to 2024) was read straight from the zip. 1,135,323 rows whose drug code is one digit repeated, a placeholder for a missing code, were dropped as the federal documentation advises: they carry a sum of $20,382.56 billion, which is not real money. A provider number counts as San Francisco when the California part of the national provider registry puts its practice address in San Francisco (252 billing numbers with drug money); California peers are all billing numbers in that registry file. A drug product is the first nine digits of the code (maker and product), package sizes added together; names come from Open Payments and Part D files that print a name beside a code. For each pharmacy (registry type beginning 3336) the drug money was added up by prescribing number over all years; rows with no prescribing number are left out of the largest-prescriber test and shown as a share.
limits: Nothing here names or counts a patient; the file withholds small cells. The file mixes pharmacy claims with drugs given in clinics and amounts health plans report, does not drop denied claims, and counts claim lines, not quantities: a line for a 90-day supply or a high dose costs more without anything being wrong. Beneficiary-months add up each month’s count of people, so a person treated every month counts twelve times. A specialty pharmacy serving people with HIV, hepatitis or cancer, a hospital clinic, a fertility or eye practice will rightly stand far above an ordinary pharmacy. 2024 is preliminary. The registry places a provider by its address today. A pharmacy inside or beside a clinic, or a specialty pharmacy serving one practice, is expected to fill mostly one prescriber’s orders; the prescribing number can be a clinic’s organisational number rather than a person. This is a pattern used to choose what to check, not evidence of steering.
